The microstructure of PWA 1480 contains a fine dispersion of coherent, cuboidal γ' with an average size of 0.5 μm and a low lattice parameter mismatch of less than 0.2%.

At low temperatures (below 760°C), the deformation behavior of <001> PWA 1480 crystals was very anisotropic, exhibiting an orientation-dependent CRSS, tension-compression asymmetry, and anisotropic strain hardening.
At high temperatures (above 820-950°C), the deformation behavior of PWA 1480 was isotropic and dominated by homogeneous γ' by-pass.
The temperature at which the transition from low to high temperature deformation behavior occurred was a function of strain rate.
The activation energy for the high temperature deformation regime was indicative of a diffusion-controlled process.
The temperature dependence of the formation of superlattice-intrinsic stacking faults was responsible for the local minimum in the CRSS of PWA 1480 at 400°C.
The cross-slip model proposed by Paidar, Pope and Vitek was found to be consistent with the proposed reversible cube cross-slip mechanism.
The Walker-Jordan constitutive model was found capable of modeling all aspects of the material anisotropy in PWA 1480.
Monotonic and cyclic tests were conducted on <001> and near-<123> PWA 1480 crystals from 20 to 1093°C and at strain rates of 0.5 and 50%/minute.
At low temperatures, the material deformed by planar octahedral slip, while at high temperatures, deformation was dominated by climb-assisted by-pass of the γ' precipitates.
The anisotropic properties of PWA 1480 at low temperatures were correlated with the ease of cube cross-slip and the number of active slip systems.
The reversible tension-compression asymmetry observed in PWA 1480 was explained by the proposed reversibility of the cube cross-slip process.
Guidelines for the numerical implementation of the Walker-Jordan constitutive model were proposed based on the identified temperature and strain rate boundaries.
The activation energy for the low temperature deformation regime was found to be independent of temperature.
No physical evidence of primary cube slip was observed in the earlier studies of single crystal superalloys like Mar-M 200.
